Why did you cancel a no annual fee credit card for life you can't get back again in future if you should ever want to? I have a couple of no annual fee credit cards I no longer use due to changes in their awards earning capacity in one case and for being a duplicated card to another that makes it obsolete in the other case, but neither costs me anything in terms of time or money to keep, so they have just been retired to a drawer, not cancelled.
Have you cut off your nose to spite your face? Did you get a momentary warm feeling of protest satisfaction wash over you when you made that phone call? Did you explain to them that your protest was in expectation they would just continue to give you free money forevermore?

Cancelling can be prudent to make most of new customer and sign on bonuses which often need to be cancelled 12months before re-applying.
I see your point, but this applies more often to bank deposit accounts rather than credit card ones. Especially true of Citibank in particular because Citibank more so than any other bank in Australia seem to keep records of past customers for an extremely long time (forever possibly). I had no relationship with Citibank in any capacity whatsoever for ~15 years but when I applied for my no annual fee Signature card, my details all came back like magic pre-populated from the Citibank database.
Just the personal details you have to submit and be checked against for each credit card application would be more than enough for me to not go cancelling credit cards on a temper-tantrum whim. These details are only bound to get more invasive and harder to pass as time goes on too.

[User #401174107 postsDRP535In the penalty box] zzyss writes...
Out of interest, say you (in general, not you personally) were applying for a loan, would you declare those cards?
Yes and I have. I have two mortgages too and during the application process, all credit cards held at that point were declared along with their credit limits.
'coz I'm thinking of cancelling my Signature after my 0% BT ends in a few months, even though it's fee free, 'coz the limit is actually very high
What do you call 'very high'? What might seem very high for you, could well be dismissed as insignificant by a bank you apply to for a home loan. This was the case for me. All my CC limits summed together (which is really the number a bank is interested in) is $93,500 which seems a ridiculous amount to me, but when I declared it on the loan application, it was pretty much dismissed as of only minor cursory interest. As long as all your credit cards are in good order for payment on time and never in arrears, then they really don't care within reason what the limits are. Those numbers are of far less importance than what you payment history is. If your record is squeeky clean, then they can see you're in control of your spending and are just gaming the system for points or whatever. The assessors are people too. They know there are people out there who use credit cards for their advantage be that points or whatever. They're not as stupid and robotic as they're often accused of being. Just because someone has a lot of credit cards with high limits, doesn't automatically equate to being a person who lives constantly riding a wave of credit until they get caught up with.
More than just raw numbers are used to decide a loan application. Surprisingly, they look at a much bigger picture than that.
